definitions.meaning: spite is rancour or resentment, a sour feeling towards someone
the bittern is the marsh bird famous for its booming call, and the old feminine ending -ess makes the female of it

explanation.surface: A question about the malice of a woman married to a loud man.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer into BITTERN, the booming marsh bird, plus the feminine suffix -ESS, as in lioness: Mrs Boomer is the female bittern.
explanation.definitionFit: Spite and rancour are both resentful ill will.

clue.text: Maker of a bundle from drink in the railways

indicators.note: in means the drink is placed inside the railway abbreviation

parts.note: BR stood for British Railways, the nationalised UK rail network
ale is a drink, a kind of beer

explanation.surface: Someone making up a parcel from what they drank on the trains.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine or person that packs hay or goods into bales, tied bundles.

clue.text: This way to Scott's Lady-of the Lake

definitions.text: This way to Scott's Lady-of the Lake

parts.words: This way to Scott's Lady-of the Lake
parts.note: Walter Scott's poem The Lady of the Lake is set in a wooded Highland district around Loch Katrine, so this signpost points there

explanation.surface: A signpost directing visitors to a heroine of Walter Scott.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's poem The Lady of the Lake (1810) made the wooded glens around Loch Katrine in Scotland a tourist destination.
explanation.definitionFit: The Highland glen region where Scott set his narrative poem around Loch Katrine.

clue.text: It involves hard work for the majority

definitions.text: It involves hard work for the majority

parts.words: It involves hard work for the majority
parts.note: the majority here is a winning margin of votes, and canvassing and campaigning are the hard work done to gain it

explanation.surface: A comment that most people have to work hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the majority' seems to mean most people, but it is a majority of votes, which campaigners work to win.
explanation.definitionFit: Campaigning and canvassing to win votes in a poll is work aimed at a majority.

clue.text: Fund that may come to be in the clutch of others

definitions.meaning: a sum of money saved for the future

definitions.text: that may come to be in the clutch of others
definitions.meaning: a clutch is a set of eggs in a nest, and a dummy egg is placed among them to encourage a hen to lay

explanation.surface: Savings that might end up in other people's hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clutch' looks like a grasping hand but is a batch of eggs; a china egg left in a nest encourages the hen to lay more.
explanation.definitionFit: Savings set aside for later, named from the decoy egg left to induce laying.

parts.note: a pen is a female swan
breakers are the waves of the sea

explanation.surface: Asks which city is home to people who break pens.
explanation.walkthrough: A pen is a female swan, and breakers are waves, the sea; together they give the city in south Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A port city on the south coast of Wales.

indicators.note: crazy means the letters of the London district are jumbled up

parts.note: the name of the south London district supplies the letters to be jumbled
AM stands for ante meridiem, the morning

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on mad nonsense heard in Balham, a south London district, before dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' scrambles BALHAM, and that pool holds the answer plus AM (morning); take AM away and the remaining four letters make the word for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Bosh and blather are both slang for empty talk or nonsense.

indicators.note: to fold cloth is to bend it into a new shape, so the letters of the fabric are rearranged

explanation.surface: Linenfold, a carved panelling pattern imitating folded cloth, found in Moscow's Red Square.
explanation.walkthrough: Linenfold is a carved wood pattern, but 'fold' splits off as the anagram signal; the definition is the Soviet founder whose embalmed body lies in the mausoleum in Red Square.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bolshevik leader whose preserved body lies in the mausoleum on Moscow's Red Square.

clue.text: The old statesman sounds hoarse my boy

indicators.note: sounds means what follows is spoken and heard rather than spelt

parts.note: hoarse means husky, and my boy is a son, so 'husky's son' is what is said

explanation.surface: An elderly politician whose voice has gone hoarse addressing a young man.
explanation.walkthrough: William Huskisson was a British statesman famous as the first person killed by a railway locomotive, in 1830.
explanation.definitionFit: A 19th-century British politician, a former President of the Board of Trade.

parts.note: super means excellent, very good
a bun is a small cake
the cakewalk was a strutting dance, so walk here stands for a dance

explanation.surface: Something very easy, a cakewalk, described as plenty good enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cake-walk' looks like an easy task, but split it gives BUN for cake and DANCE for walk, since the cakewalk was a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A great excess, more than enough, is an abundance beyond plenty.

definitions.meaning: the caterpillars of geometer moths, which move by arching their bodies into a loop
fighter pilots in aerial dogfights fly loops, so they are ones who loop

explanation.surface: Asks whether caterpillars are to be found in fights between dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: A dogfight is an air battle between fighter planes, whose pilots loop the loop; the same word names the inchworm caterpillars that move in loops.
explanation.definitionFit: Caterpillars of the geometer moth are called loopers or inchworms from their arching gait.

clue.text: Chemical substance ' seen back of the sun by the pupil

parts.note: alum is a chemical compound, a double sulphate used in dyeing and tanning

indicators.note: read as 'the sun backwards', the word sun is reversed rather than its last letter taken

explanation.surface: A chemistry lesson where a pupil sees some compound behind the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back of the sun' looks like the last letter N, but it means SUN written backwards, NUS, after ALUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A former pupil or student of a school is an alumnus; here the old usage is any pupil.

parts.note: the Wars of the Roses were an old English war named after flowers; the plants that bloom with that flower are woody shrubs

explanation.surface: A mention of antiquated wartime underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomers suggests baggy knickers, but here they are plants that bloom; the old war is the Wars of the Roses, named after the white and red rose badges.
explanation.definitionFit: The flowering shrubs that carry the bloom which named the Wars of the Roses.

parts.note: a word borrowed from French for weary boredom and lack of interest

explanation.surface: A comment on the supposed Gallic lack of enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' means the word itself is a borrowing from French, not that the boredom belongs to the French.
explanation.definitionFit: The French loanword for listless weariness, a lack of any interest.

definitions.meaning: Donizetti's opera Lucia di Lammermoor has a heroine named Lucia; her brother would bear the masculine form of her name
in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure the fantastic gentleman of Vienna lives under the rule of the deputy Angelo

explanation.surface: Asks about a sibling from an operatic estate serving beneath a Shakespearean deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading takes Lucia's name and makes it masculine, so a brother of hers would be named that, though in the opera her brother is Enrico. Lammermoor is misspelt as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: A masculine form of the opera heroine's name is also the character in Measure for Measure governed by Angelo.

clue.text: Take down bag from rack? Not if one's for the capital

definitions.text: Not if one's for the capital

parts.note: to lower is to take something down
a case is a bag for carrying things

explanation.surface: Instructions to lift a bag from a luggage rack, unless one is travelling to London.
explanation.walkthrough: A printer's type cases sat on a rack: capitals in the upper case and small letters in the lower one, so these letters are not for capitals.
explanation.definitionFit: Small letters, as opposed to capital letters, were kept in the lower of the compositor's type cases.

parts.note: split as 'corn wall', the walls that hold grain are part of a storehouse for harvested grain

explanation.surface: A geography question about which larger whole the county of Cornwall belongs to.
explanation.walkthrough: Cornwall is the county at England's south-west tip; split into CORN WALL it becomes the wall of a grain store.
explanation.definitionFit: Storehouses for threshed grain have walls that hold the corn.

parts.note: Émile Coué taught self-help by repeating 'Every day in every way I am getting better and better', so his followers worked at getting better

explanation.surface: Asks about labourers serving a 1920s French self-help movement.
explanation.walkthrough: Couéism was the self-suggestion method of the French pharmacist Émile Coué, built on the mantra that one gets better every day. The OCR text drops the accent mark printed on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: People who work at making themselves better, as Coué's mantra urged.

clue.text: Are we less lenient' to a little grey home-owner ?

parts.note: taken as written
sterner means stricter, less lenient

explanation.surface: Wonders whether we are being too harsh towards the owner of a small grey house.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition recalls the old song 'A Little Grey Home in the West', so its owner is someone from the west.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's little grey home is in the West, so its owner is someone living in the West.

clue.text: It's for no one in Scotland to deprive one of capital abroad

parts.note: na is the Scots word for no, as signalled by 'in Scotland'
I is the Roman numeral one
to rob is to deprive someone of something
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A Scot declares it is not for anyone to strip a person of their money while abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' seems to be money, but it is a capital city abroad, Kenya's. 'in Scotland' marks NA as the Scots form of no.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital city of Kenya, in East Africa.

clue.text: Make a come-back — who, the clergyman ?

definitions.meaning: to come back to a place or go there again
asked who it is, one replies '...?', guessing it is the reverend gentleman

explanation.surface: Someone returning, and a puzzled voice asking whether the caller is the vicar.
explanation.walkthrough: Rev is short for Reverend, a clergyman; the answer split up reads 'Rev, is it?', a reply to 'who?'.
explanation.definitionFit: To return to a place, going there again.

clue.text: It discomposes a pi nun to do as Desdemona bade Emilia

indicators.note: to discompose is to disarrange, so the letters of these words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Something unsettles a pious nun while carrying out an instruction from Shakespeare's Othello.
explanation.walkthrough: In Othello Act 4 Scene 3 Desdemona says to her maid Emilia 'Prithee, unpin me', asking her to undo her clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Desdemona asks Emilia to undo the pins of her dress, to unfasten it.

parts.note: read as a comparative of binding it is a word like 'more robing'; really it is an attendant who wraps another person in robes

explanation.surface: A companion who is more obligated or committed than another.
explanation.walkthrough: The '-er' of a comparative ('more binding') doubles as the '-er' of an agent noun: one who robes another, wrapping and dressing them.
explanation.definitionFit: An attendant who dresses someone in robes, wrapping them up.

clue.text: Gamely attempts global lowering at a stroke

definitions.text: Gamely attempts global lowering at a stroke

parts.words: Gamely attempts global lowering at a stroke
parts.note: in game shooting the guns stand in screened shooting stands and try to bring down birds with a single shot; 'Gamely' points to game birds

explanation.surface: A brave effort to cut something worldwide in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gamely' means at game, as in grouse shooting, where guns shoot from screened stands called butts on the moor.
explanation.definitionFit: The screened shooting positions on a grouse moor from which the guns fire.

clue.text: Bad French wine I'd get with credit-notes is offensive

indicators.note: bad suggests something spoilt or wrong, so the French word is rearranged

parts.note: vin is the French word for wine
taken as written without the apostrophe
IOUs are written promises to pay, notes recording credit given

explanation.surface: Poor-quality French wine bought on promissory notes is nasty stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges VIN (French wine) into INV; then come ID and IOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Invidious things give offence or provoke resentment, so they are objectionable.

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed, so the letters of the word are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Anguished souls, so theatrically left on their own.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a Latin stage direction meaning a character is alone on stage, the male counterpart of sola.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin stage direction marking a male character by himself on stage.

definitions.meaning: in The Tempest the usurping brother of Prospero is a famous traitor to his own family
the Italian name is a stock one for an ice-cream seller, and it also belongs to Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice

explanation.surface: A complaint about a notoriously unreliable seller of ice cream.
explanation.walkthrough: The same Italian name serves Shakespeare's treacherous brother in The Tempest, the title merchant of Venice, and a stereotyped Italian ice-cream vendor.
explanation.definitionFit: A common Italian name used by Shakespeare for a traitorous duke and for the Venetian merchant, and for many ice-cream sellers.

indicators.note: bad here suggests letters that are spoilt, so they are rearranged

parts.note: these two words supply the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Launce, the clownish servant in The Two Gentlemen of Verona, sees a bad lad stranded.
explanation.walkthrough: Launce looks like Shakespeare's comic servant, but it is the small eel-like fish of that name that burrows in sand.
explanation.definitionFit: The launce is another name for the small burrowing fish of sandy shores.

parts.note: in Tom Brown's Schooldays Tom's friend is a boy whose name is a point of the compass, the opposite one to the home in 17 across

explanation.surface: A remark that a particular pupil came from somewhere surprising.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Brown's Schooldays, set at Rugby School, gives Tom a friend called by a compass point; the 'Yet' is the contrast between his name and the opposite direction in 17.
explanation.definitionFit: The compass direction opposite to west, which is also the surname of Tom Brown's schoolfriend.

clue.text: Old theatre wigs for winning girls ?

parts.note: the Vic is short for the Old Vic, a famous London theatre
tresses are locks of hair, such as wigs supply

explanation.surface: Wigs from a historic playhouse used to dress female winners.
explanation.walkthrough: The Old Vic is a famous London theatre; 'old theatre' also hints at actresses.
explanation.definitionFit: A victor is a winner; the feminine form with -ess names women or girls who win.
